title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge generative artificial intelligence poses for school mathematics: many traditional tasks can now be solved automatically, reducing students’ need to interpret situations, make decisions, or validate results. The author asks how mathematics teaching can preserve students’ mathematical activity and epistemic control in post-AI contexts.

The paper analyzes a classroom experience in secondary education in which open mathematical tasks were implemented as a didactic response to generative AI. The intervention was mediated by a regulatory device called COMPAS, which organizes work into phases of understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, producing and exploring results, analysis and validation, and socialization/synthesis. The study is qualitative and descriptive-interpretive, based on student written work, classroom interaction records, and teacher-researcher observations.

The context is a single secondary-school mathematics classroom in Peru. The paper argues that open tasks with explicit didactic regulation can prevent premature task closure and keep AI in a subordinate role, used for exploration or checking rather than as a source of definitive answers. The main conclusion is that students can retain epistemic control, mathematical agency, and active participation when task design requires assumptions, modeling, and validation. The paper also notes that tensions between AI-generated solutions and student models can be productively used to support discussion and critical validation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative descriptive–interpretive classroom study, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation. It provides rich contextual evidence but does not meet RCT/QED credibility criteria and does not report causal effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests pedagogically meaningful benefits for mathematical agency and validation practices, but the findings are local, qualitative, and non-quantified. There is no reported effect size, so impact is promising but unclear at the population level.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that, in a secondary-school classroom experience using open mathematical tasks mediated by COMPAS, students maintained epistemic control of the mathematical activity despite the presence of generative AI. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive rather than causal; no effect size was reported, but the observed outcomes included interpretation, modeling, and validation of solutions rather than passive acceptance of AI outputs.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of student written work, classroom interactions, and teacher-observer notes focusing on mathematical agency, modeling, and validation

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that open tasks plus explicit didactic regulation supported students’ mathematical agency, argumentation, and critical validation of results. Students were described as actively formulating assumptions, comparing models, and questioning AI-generated answers, indicating strengthened critical thinking and metacognitive regulation, though no quantitative effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative observation of agency, argumentation, and validation practices during task resolution
